title: Quantum Spins Move Centimeter‑Scale Object for First Time—Breakthrough in Quantum Mechanics】
body:
A team of physicists has demonstrated for the first time that the intrinsic spin of electrons can be harnessed to move a macroscopic object—a tiny silica sphere roughly one centimetre across—by more than a nanometre. The breakthrough, achieved by coupling the quantum‑mechanical magnetic moment of an ensemble of electron spins to the mechanical vibrations of the sphere, marks a watershed moment in the quest to bridge the gap between the quantum and classical worlds and opens new avenues for ultra‑sensitive sensing, quantum information processing, and tests of fundamental physics.

The experiment, carried out at the University of Sydney’s Centre for Quantum Computation and Communication Technology, employed a hybrid system in which a dense cloud of nitrogen‑vacancy (NV) centres—defects in diamond that host unpaired electron spins—was embedded in a thin layer of diamond attached to the surface of the silica bead. By illuminating the NV centres with a carefully tuned microwave field, the researchers induced a collective precession of the electron spins, creating a tiny, oscillating magnetic field. This field, in turn, exerted a torque on the bead, causing it to vibrate at its resonant frequency. Sensitive interferometric measurements recorded a displacement of the bead’s centre of mass that exceeded the thermal noise floor, confirming that the spin ensemble had indeed transferred angular momentum to the macroscopic object.

The result is more than a laboratory curiosity. For decades, physicists have been able to manipulate individual quantum systems—single atoms, ions, photons—but scaling those effects up to objects visible to the naked eye has proved elusive. Prior attempts relied on radiation pressure from lasers or electrostatic forces, which, while effective, do not directly exploit the magnetic properties of matter at the quantum level. By demonstrating that electron spin—a purely quantum attribute—can generate a measurable mechanical force on a centimetre‑scale body, the study provides a proof‑of‑concept for “spin‑mechanics,” a nascent field that could complement existing optomechanical platforms.

The implications for precision metrology are immediate. Spin‑based forces are intrinsically linked to magnetic fields, suggesting that spin‑mechanical devices could serve as ultra‑high‑resolution magnetometers capable of detecting minute variations in magnetic environments, from neuronal activity in the brain to subtle geological signatures. Moreover, the ability to couple spins to mechanical motion offers a new route to quantum transduction, where information encoded in solid‑state qubits can be transferred to phonons—quantized vibrations—enabling hybrid quantum networks that combine the long coherence times of spin systems with the long‑distance transport capabilities of mechanical waves.

Beyond applications, the experiment touches on deep questions about the boundary between quantum superposition and classical determinism. By scaling up the system while preserving quantum coherence long enough to produce a detectable mechanical response, the researchers have taken a step toward testing collapse models that posit a fundamental limit to quantum behaviour as objects grow in mass. Future iterations that increase the number of spins, reduce thermal noise, or employ levitated particles could push the displacement into the sub‑nanometre regime, where the influence of quantum back‑action becomes observable.

Looking ahead, the team plans to refine the coupling efficiency by engineering diamond films with higher NV‑centre densities and by cooling the mechanical resonator to its quantum ground state. Such advances could enable the creation of entangled states between distant spin ensembles mediated by a shared mechanical mode, a capability that would be a cornerstone for distributed quantum computing. As the line between the quantum and macroscopic realms continues to blur, the ability to command the motion of everyday objects with the spin of electrons may soon transition from a laboratory demonstration to a cornerstone technology in quantum engineering.
